mnemonic: 한국 means Korea, but there's more to this little word than meets the eye: its official name is 대한민국 (Republic of Korea), but in casual conversations its citizens use 우리나라 (our country) affectionately when talking about their homeland.
examples: Some bits of history: The English word Korea actually comes from 고려 (Goryeo), an ancient Korean dynasty that stand from 918 to 1392! And before that, the country was ruled by the famous 조선 (Joseon) Dynasty (1392–1897).So 고려, 조선, 대한민국 (1897-1910)... refer to different historical periods of Korea.
- 우리나라는 아름다워요. = Our country is beautiful.
- 저는 한국에 살아요. = I live in Korea.
- 대한민국의 수도는 서울이에요. = The capital of the Republic of Korea is Seoul.

mnemonic: The establishment that serves coffee is said 카페 (sounds just like “café”), meanwhile the product itself is said 커피 (kopi).
examples: I used to confuse 카페 and 커피, maybe a way of saving memory of my primitive Korean-mode-brain. Also because in Spanish I find it hilarious to call the establishment the exact way we call the product and the establishment:
-¡Te veo en el café! = 카페에서 만나요!
-No me gusta el café de ese café. = 저는 그 카페 커피를 좋아하지 않아요.
(I don’t like the coffee from that café.)
See? In spanish it sounds weird to repeat the same word for place and product, so we distinguish it by calling it cafetería = 커피숍 (coffee shop) / 커피 가게 (coffee shop).
